messages.subject: update on variational inference
messages.body_plain:
hey guys,

happy 2015!

i'm currently working on exposing the parameters of
the variational algorithm to the cmdline. this whole
gm/command structure is really powerful.

that aside, i have two goals that might be worth a
chat with you guys (at least via email/here):

1. robustfication/convergence: i forget who wrote
the optimization stuff, but i think for variational
our best bet is the tol_param strategy (norm of
difference of parameters across interations). i'd
love to hear thoughts on this, especially since
the variational objective function *and* its
gradients are both noisy.

part of this will also be initialization. i'm finding
that our algorithm can be sensitive to bad inits
especially if a stan model has a lot of transformations.
thoughts/strategies would be welcome here too.

2. reporting/output. the idea that many of you
suggested was to draw from the final configuration
of the variational gaussians and transform these
back to the unconstrained domain, then report
quantiles like in sampling etc.

if this is going to be useful for EP etc. then it might
be worth coordinating the design (by which i mean
how it should fit in Stan). if folks can help me
with that, i'll try my best to write decent code to
fill in the rest.

cheers,
alp

You can scale down the range of random inits to keep
initial values on the unconstrained scale close to 0.
That is 0 for unconstrained parameters, 1 for positive
constrained (exp inverse transform), 0.5 for parameters
constrained between 0 and 1 (inverse logit), symmetric
simplexes, unit correlation covariance matrices.  We've
generally found those to be better behaved.

It also helps if the data are reasonably scaled.

I do think Matt would have some insight into initialization for VB, given that he’s thought a lot about initialization (in various contexts) and VB (in various contexts).

messages.body_plain:
Taking this over to stan-dev now...

So I'm not sure I follow the pattern with the nested memory stuff, but here is what happens:

- initialize_state_random first calls stan::model::gradient() which calls stan::agrad::gradient() which evaluates the gradient but cleans up with stan::agrad::recover_memory_nested()
- recover_memory_nested() calls delete on the elements of var_alloc_stack_ but doesn't clear it so var_alloc_stack now has some defunct pointers in it.
- the optimizer then calls stan::model::log_prob_grad() which evaluates the gradient and cleans up with stan::agrad::recover_memory() which, at this point tries to delete defunct pointers on var_alloc_stack_.

My hunch is that var_alloc_stack_ needs to be cleared (or truncated) in recover_memory_nested(), but I don't understand the nested memory stuff so I didn't want to just dive in.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject_clean: out of domain errors (e.g., with CDFs)
messages.body_plain:
We have the general problem that for many functions, the mathematical
range exceeds the floating-point range, either for the function itself
or for its derivative.

For example, the normal CDF only works in roughly the range (-25,25)
or so.  But the limit for the value is 0 to the left and 1
to the right, with a limit of 0 for the derivatives.  For the inverse gamma
CDF where Rob ran into this issue, as y->0, the value goes to 0 and the
derivative to +infinity.

I think the problem should be framed in terms of impliciations for
optimization and HMC.  For gradient based optimization, whatever
parameter hits a 0 derivative won't move.  In HMC, it'll just have
0 potential, but it'll still move because of the random kinetic
energy --- but it'll never make a U-turn.  In both, infinite values
or derivatives wind up leaving you stuck where you're at.

QUESTION:  What should we do when called with a var/fvar out of domain?

1.  Raise an exception.

2.  Return whatever the limit is (+inf, -inf, 0).

3.  Sometimes 1, sometimes 2, depending on the limit in question.

4.  None of the above;  we should _____________.

I believe whatever we do we want to doc it in general and carry it through
all of our functions.

- Bob

If the file is in your .gitignore or more appropriately in your
.git/info/exclude (e.g. so only for your local repo only), then it
won't be wiped out when changing branches.  The latter won't wipe it
out even if it's not .gitignore'd in the new branch.  (If it's in
.gitignore on both branches it should not be wiped out.)

Another option is to use smudge/clean filters locally and a
.gitattributes filter for make/local.  That's a more correct but more
complicated option.

Yet another option is to "git stash save -u" before switching
branches, then "git stash pop" after, but that could have unintended
side effects.

messages.subject: 2 kinds of error checking
messages.body_plain:
I find with a perusal of the source code that there are two kinds of
error checks.

+ Checks that only need to be done once to verify that the model can be
evaluated (like matrix conformability checking).

a covariance matrix is positive definite).

every iteration. Do we have a plan to split up these checks into
separate parts of the generated source code?

On Thu, Jan 22, 2015 at 8:35 AM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:
> I find with a perusal of the source code that there are two kinds of
> error checks.
>
> + Checks that only need to be done once to verify that the model can be
> evaluated (like matrix conformability checking).
>
> + Checks that need to be done at every iteration (like checking whether
> a covariance matrix is positive definite).
>
> Currently, it appears that both of these types of checks are done at
> every iteration. Do we have a plan to split up these checks into
> separate parts of the generated source code?
>

We've thought about splitting it up, but not in the generated source code. There really isn't much in the generated code that needs to be separated.

If we were to split it up, one way to do it would be to add a bool template parameter that indicates whether checks that can be done once needs to be done. Of course, this isn't fool-proof: since Stan has conditionals, we might run into a problem if we branched differently later.

Even if we didn't split apart the checking, with the pull request, we'll be able to handle the errors differently, which would improve the behavior of Stan for the users. We'd be able to stop immediately after catching one of the first types of errors.

With that said, we've gone back and forth about trying to turn off checking. Most of the checks are fast and you won't notice the impact of removing checks like checking matrix sizes, checking nan, etc. (well... after the pull request that's one now that fixes the std::string issue) There are a few checks that are slow and can use some work. One reason for not doing what I suggested above is that it adds complexity to our code. A lot of complexity. Unless we have a lot of speed benefit, I don't think we should go down this path. If you or anyone can show that these actually have an large impact on models, then I'm all ears.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for bringing the discussion onto stan-dev.

The most time consuming checks are the ones that test things
like positive-definiteness of a matrix or even symmetry.
For data, these are done only once.  For parameters, they
have to be done every iteration.

It's technically impossible to pre-check with our current language,
but explaining why is a bit of digression into CS theory.

Because Stan is Turing complete (a consequence of having
general while loops and assignment), it's impossible to
figure out even whether a statement will get executed (the
problem is technically what is known as "undecidable" in
computational theory).

Without worrying about really hard cases, consider
this program:

parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
  ...

model {
  int n;
  if (theta > 0.99)
     n <- 20;
  else
     n <- 10;
  ...
  tail(y,n) ~ normal(tail(mu,n), sigma);

the problem is that whether the call to normal is sound or not
depends on a run-time choice based on the value of theta.  So it
can't just be done once.

Similarly, we have a requirement that sigma > 0, but due to
problems with floating point underflow, we can wind up with sigma == 0
on some iterations.  So those tests have to remain at runtime.

Now the problem is that you'd think indexing would be checkable
ahead of time, but now the index depends on a parameter.  Whether the
tail statement and hence the normal are well formed will depend on
n.

We are considering eliminating this behavior by making (theta > 0.99)
an illegal statement if theta is not data.  Then we would be able to
tell what gets executed by running once because the data would never
change.  This is something we're thinking about going forward.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
I did some work implementing CVODE as an ODE solver in Stan. CVODE is a really great solver, the implementation has been around for many years and based on even older fortran code.
It can deal with stiff ODEs and with failure cases when there are instabilities.

I'm collaborating with statisticians in Pharma as well as academics with lots of ODE models that don't fit in the box of nice models that RK45 can deal with. Most of the work up till now has been using custom build software, but I also would like to contribute the knowledge gained with the wonderful effort of Stan.

Unfortunately, CVODE is obviously a little bit more heavy for simpler models such as the harmonic oscillator or Lorenz. But there is definitely a gain with more complex models as it can deal with stiff models and usually take large time steps. I'm now trying to get the authorization from my collaborators to release some of the models and the data that we are working with to the Stan community. Those definitely require a more advanced solver.

I'm also working on an implementation of a more advanced technique to compute the gradients: there are cases when the sensitivity approach is too expensive. But this might take a little while longer to complete.

Would you be interested in this work or discussing it further?

As for lsoda/cvoda, both solvers are based on the same algorithms (BDF or Adams-Moulton). Both have also been around for a long long time and started out as Fortran code. I believe CVODE is a reimplementation (also geared towards parallelism) whereas lsoda is an automatic translation to C.
They are basically the de-facto standard for any ODE solving (except for the easy cases). I have a slight preference for CVODE, but I would say there is no real difference.
As for the jacobians, both packages can compute the jacobians using finite differencing but the user can also provide it as a function in dense or sparse format. I don't think that the Adams-Moulton algorithm uses Jacobians, since it's basically a Runge-Kutta + correction. For the sensitivity solution, the jacobian might involve higher-order derivation of the righ-hand side but FD might be fine. But there are different ways to go about this.

Tom

another project) that updates from the GitHub repositories any time a
new release is tagged.  This could go into Jenkins or just a
web/service hook from GitHub.

something together.  If anyone has packages for existing distributions
already made, please send them to me for inclusion.  It'll save me
some time testing.  For now, I have an Arch package that I'll update

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I've put my latest version on my github fork: https://github.com/tomhaber/stan/tree/cvode

I just added the code providing jacobians to CVODE as discussed previously: instead of CVODE doing finite differencing, this code does finite differencing internally for computing the hessians. It can exploit the structure of the jacobian to compute it much faster: should be in order of #parameters faster.
When/if higher-order autodiff becomes available, this internal finite differencing can then be easily replaced.

The simple unit tests seem to work, but I should run a test on my other models as well.

The linking would be something that you guys could definitely help with. I'm currently using an ugly hack to completely avoid it. The header-only thing makes it a little hard. When I briefly looked at it, I could only see a possibility of adding it into the R binding code.

For now, it is more of a prototype. I use a wrapper that I made to hide any ode solver, but it might not make sense now (Unless you consider other ode solvers at some point). The implementation can be cleaned up/simplified otherwise.

Tom

The current coupled system uses std::vector a lot which doesn't fit nicely with CVODE's C interface, so at the moment it does some extra copying which isn't really required. Additionally it uses CVODE's built-in FD to compute Jacobians, which might still needs to be replaced as it would make the method much more efficient. Without resorting to higher-order autodiff, applying FD outside of CVODE could be beneficial because of the structure of the jacobian. Since CVODE has no idea about this structure it needs to do tons of extra work. I'll look into this next week.
